title: Acharei Mot: after the deaths (Leviticus 16:1)
hook: the Yom Kippur service is given right after Aaron's loss

segments.voice: Yesterday, Metzora ended with a person walked home, step by step. Your line was there is a way back. Today, a new portion that looks back before it looks forward.

Some dates in a family's calendar carry two things at once. A wedding planned for the month after a funeral. A holiday that falls on the anniversary of a loss. They can't be separated, and after a while families stop trying. The next portion of Leviticus is called Acharei Mot, after the death. It's where the Torah lays out the service for Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. And it doesn't begin with the day, or the rules. It reaches back six chapters, to Aaron's terrible day.
screen: `TWO THINGS ON ONE DATE.` → `ACHAREI MOT: AFTER THE DEATH.` → `BACK TO AARON'S LOSS.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God spoke to Moses "after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before the LORD, and died." Chapters of skin, birth and houses have come in between, but the Torah ties the Day of Atonement back to Nadav and Avihu. Why mention the deaths here? Rashi compares it to two doctors visiting a sick man. The first says: don't eat cold food, don't lie in a damp place. The second says the same, and adds: so you don't die the way so-and-so died. The second warning lands harder. The rules for entering the holy place come with the memory of the sons still fresh. The Jerusalem Talmud asks why their deaths are placed next to Yom Kippur, and answers that the death of the righteous, like Yom Kippur, brings atonement. Whatever one makes of that, it's a striking pairing: loss doesn't sit outside the holy day. It's written into its first line. And here is how it's lived. In traditional synagogues, this very chapter is read on Yom Kippur morning. And on Yom Kippur, Ashkenazi communities say Yizkor, the memorial prayer for those they've lost. The Day of Atonement makes room for the dead. After grief, atonement: not instead of grief, but after it, and with it.
screen: `AFTER THE DEATH OF AARON'S SONS.` · `RASHI: THE SECOND DOCTOR'S WARNING.` · `LOSS IN THE FIRST LINE.` · `YIZKOR ON YOM KIPPUR.` · then, large: `AFTER GRIEF, ATONEMENT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a loss you've carried, a person, a time of life, a hope that didn't happen, and don't rush past the sadness of it. Then gently ask what it has taught you about what matters; if nothing comes, that's all right, grief teaches on its own schedule. If you pray, remember the one you lost in your prayers.
